summary: Deep dive on small-packet multiplexing effects on p95/p99, KV cache backpressure in VPC/on-prem topologies, and streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs. Focus: reproduce SignalFlow microbursts, identify shard hotness, and plan bench runs with Redwood Private nodes.
topics: VPC/on-prem network hops and firewall behavior
questions: What's the delta in p99 for streaming vs non-streaming at 1k qps with 8-16 token replies?
How does Redwood handle KV cache backpressure during fanout bursts?
What telemetry is available inside Private for tracing inter-node hop latency?
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to dig into these repeat microbursts you've seen and capture specifics — small packets, many concurrent streams, and the p95/p99 blow-ups.
[00:18] Amir (Staff SRE): yeah sorry about the noisy metrics in the ticket — we noticed spikes only when clients multiplex ~200-400 tiny prompts per session, each response 10-20 tokens. p95 is fine but p99 jumps to 600-900ms intermittently.
[00:36] Priya (SE): ok that's classic small-packet effect plus application-level concurrency. two immediate hypotheses: 1) TCP/TLS small-packet inefficiency and Nagle interactions across the VPC path, 2) KV cache hotkeys causing internal queuing.
[00:54] Lina (ML Platform): we do also see higher CPU on the edge proxies during those blasts; sometimes a single KV shard goes to 100% and others are idle.
[01:10] Jordan: do you have shard mapping? are you using consistent hashing or sticky routing?
[01:16] Amir: we shard by conversation-id mod N, that's sticky. thought that would be fine but one customer tenant tends to create many tiny threads, so it concentrates.
[01:28] Priya: ok sticky explains hotspot. with sticky shard you get uneven distribution when use-case has many small very active keys. that can create head-of-line queuing in the runtime's KV transport layer.
[01:40] Ravi (CTO): question: is that queuing in the Redwood runtime or our network ingress? we have a separate VPC peered to Redwood Private node.
[01:48] Priya: good question. there are multiple places: 1) egress queue on your edge proxy, 2) serialization and TLS session management per connection, 3) runtime per-shard worker queues. we need traces from both sides.
[02:04] Jordan: quick note — streaming vs non-streaming also changes where you accumulate latency. streaming reduces per-response latency when you can emit tokens earlier, but it increases pressure on small-packet throughput since you send more frames.
[02:18] Amir: we've tried both; non-streaming p95 is lower in steady-state, but streaming had better median during heavy load, yet p99 got worse sometimes. seems inconsistent.
[02:29] Priya: that matches expectations. streaming pushes more frequent writes and can amplify Nagle/ACK coalescing behavior unless TCP_NODELAY is set end-to-end. also TLS record sizes matter — if streaming uses many small TLS records you'll pay CPU and syscalls.
[02:44] Amir: any workaround short-term? besides rearchitecting clients?
[02:48] Priya: a few tactical knobs: add client-side batching (coalesce micro-prompts for same shard), enable TCP_NODELAY where safe, or increase concurrency limits with adaptive backpressure. long term, rebalance shards or use a rip-pled hashing scheme to avoid tenant hotkeys.
[03:06] Lina: we don't want to change clients quickly — many third-party integrations — so infrastructure mitigations preferred.
[03:12] Priya: in that case we can do two things on Redwood Private: 1) tune the KV transport to process small packets more efficiently (reduce per-record checks, enable splice/zero-copy where possible), 2) configure per-shard worker scaling so hot shards get temporary workers. both require bench validation.
[03:30] Jordan: let's capture an experiment plan. Priya, can you outline the bench scenarios?
[03:34] Priya: yes. scenario A: 1k qps steady, 8 token responses, non-streaming. scenario B: 1k qps, same payloads, streaming with token flush every 4 tokens. scenario C: 2k burst with multiplexing 200 concurrent tiny sequences per client. For each: cold cache, warm cache, and hot-key concentrated runs. measure p50/p95/p99, CPU, net packets per second, TLS record sizes, and per-shard queue length.
[04:04] Amir: that sounds good. are we able to collect per-hop traces inside the Private node? we have limited visibility after peering.
[04:11] Priya: Redwood Private includes a tracing hook — we can enable hop-level timings and VXLAN/TCP tail histograms. requires an agent enablement in the control plane; we can do that for the bench window.
[04:22] Ravi: do you need any firewall/open port changes?
[04:24] Priya: only for the trace agent endpoint (TLS) — we'll provide exact ports. Amir, you mentioned earlier firewall rules, right?
[04:30] Amir: yes, will attach the current ruleset after this call.
[04:34] Jordan: let's talk about quantization/CPU effects for small responses — you suggested earlier that quantized paths reduce per-token CPU; is that material here?
[04:43] Priya: depends. for 8-20 token replies, the kernel launch overhead and tensor copy matter less than TLS/syscall overhead. Quantization reduces model compute but doesn't change the small-packet networking cost. For p99, model compute could matter if your sequences spike longer; but for microbursts it's mostly I/O and KV lookup latency.
[05:02] Lina: so quantization is lower priority for this specific class of spike?
[05:05] Priya: correct — focus on KV and network first. If bench shows model tail contributions >30% of p99, then we revisit quantization and batching inside the runtime.
[05:16] Amir: what about batching? we tried turning on longer batching windows to aggregate small requests — but that increases median noticeably.
[05:24] Priya: batching reduces unit cost and can flatten p99 if you can afford latency tradeoff. For your product we need to balance SLOs: maybe dynamic batching — small latency SLOs during interactive periods and batch during offline ingestion. Redwood supports dynamic batching profiles mapped by route.
[05:42] Jordan: can we do smart fallbacks? e.g., if a shard is overloaded, route to a compatible lower-cost model replica?
[05:49] Priya: yes, routing policies can fallback to a model variant but that impacts output quality. We can set automatic fallback only for extremely high-latency windows and monitor regressions with a lightweight eval set. We'll show an example in the runbook.
[06:02] Ravi: curious about cost implications: streaming increased egress and CPU. Any rough numbers?
[06:08] Jordan: we'll produce a delta table — rough order: streaming increases CPU cycles by ~10-20% in signal workloads due to TLS and per-chunk processing and may increase egress small-packet overhead. We'll quantify after we run the harness.
[06:20] Priya: also remember KV cache hit ratio is a huge cost lever — a warm cache reduces both latency and cost. The bench should include realistic TTLs and cache churn.
[06:31] Amir: note: our TTLs are 30s currently; many conversations are single-turn. maybe extend to 5m?
[06:37] Lina: we can try increasing TTL, but memory footprint rises. we prefer sharding changes first.
[06:41] Priya: tradeoffs: longer TTLs smooth bursts but increase hot-spot persistence. dynamic TTL based on key access patterns sometimes works: shorter TTL for idle keys, extended TTL for keys on consistent heavy access.
[06:55] Jordan: ok let's zoom into network hops — Amir, you mentioned an odd NAT behavior in one region?
[07:00] Amir: yes in eu-west-2 we saw NAT gateway timeouts occasionally; connections are reestablished and that caused transient 1-2s spikes.
[07:08] Priya: NAT timeouts are brutal for small TCP sessions. Strategies: keep-alive tuning, connection pooling, or use a VPC endpoint with direct peering to Redwood to avoid NAT. Also check MTU fragmentation across the path — sometimes TLS record fragmentation coupled with MTU causes retries.
[07:26] Amir: we'll check MTU and current NAT config.
[07:30] Ravi: what's the recommended peering topology?
[07:32] Priya: direct VPC peering to Redwood Private or AWS PrivateLink if available. That removes gateway NATs and reduces per-connection churn. If that's not possible, make sure keepalive and connection recycle parameters are tuned and consider sidecar connection pools.
[07:45] Jordan: we should call out measurement endpoints: 1) app-level logs with request ids 2) runtime per-shard queue histograms 3) OS-level socket queue sizes and TLS record histograms.
[07:56] Priya: yes we'll push a minimal tracing manifest to your team that captures those metrics. we'll also add a lightweight packet-size histogram to see how many sub-150B TLS records occur.
[08:08] Amir: that would be helpful.
[08:10] Jordan: ok next, timeline — we want a bench window next week. Amir, is that feasible?
[08:14] Amir: yes if we can get the manifest and the ports. I'll clear a bench window on 2027-08-04.
[08:19] Priya: perfect. I'll plan to run initial runs and share raw traces; then we'll iterate.
[08:24] Lina: any quick wins we should do before bench?
[08:27] Priya: set TCP_NODELAY on client side for streaming, ensure connection pooling instead of opening new sockets per micro-prompt, and check MTU. Those are low-effort.
[08:36] Amir: we'll push an immediate change to enable pooling and TCP_NODELAY on a canary subset.
[08:40] Jordan: great. before we wrap, recap of concrete deliverables?
[08:44] Priya: I'll run bench scenarios A/B/C and post results, including p50/p95/p99, TLS record histos, per-shard queue histos, and packet rates.
[08:51] Jordan: I'll send pricing delta and the runbook for streaming fallbacks and routing policies.
[08:55] Amir: I'll share topology and firewall rules and enable a bench window on 2027-08-04.
[08:59] Ravi: good. thanks everyone. one more ask — can Redwood recommend a sharding pattern that reduces tenant concentration?
[09:05] Priya: yes — use hopscotch or vbucket style hashing with virtual nodes so tenant keys spread across more physical shards; we'll include a config example.
[09:14] Jordan: awesome. we'll follow up in email with attachments. thanks all.
[09:18] Amir: thanks.
[09:20] [END]
notes: Shared artifacts referenced: bench-harness repo link (will be sent), streaming-fallback-runbook.pdf (to be attached), SignalFlow VPC diagram (customer to share).
